item.title: CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation
item.content:encoded:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today issued an interpretation (“Interpretation”) of the requirement that designated contract markets (“DCMs”) provide competitive, open, fair, and impartial access to their members and persons with trading privileges under Commission Regulation 38.151(b) (“Impartial Access Requirements”). 

“Derivatives markets must operate on a uniform basis at a national scale in order to achieve the purposes set out in the Commodity Exchange Act,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “Geographic access restrictions are inconsistent with those purposes and the Act’s impartial access requirements.”

DCMs must cease domestic geographic restrictions that violate the Impartial Access Requirements within 30 days, or else submit to the Division of Market Oversight (“Division”) an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. Further, within 30 days, DCMs should ensure that intermediaries accessing their markets are not impeding and are complying with the DCM’s Impartial Access Requirements, or else submit to the Division an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. The Commission will consider the facts and circumstances of any particular case in connection with potential Commission action.

item.title: EDX Markets Partners With BitSafe To Launch CBTC Trading, Expanding Institutional Access To Bitcoin On Canton Network
item.content:encoded:
EDX Markets, a digital asset technology firm that combines an institutional-only trading venue with a central clearinghouse, today announced a partnership with BitSafe to launch spot trading of CBTC, BitSafe’s Bitcoin-backed digital asset on the Canton Network. The listing marks CBTC’s first availability on a centralized exchange, enabling eligible clients to buy and sell the asset against U.S. dollars through EDX’s marketplace.

CBTC is backed 1:1 by Bitcoin and designed to bring its value into Canton’s financial ecosystem. Through CBTC, clients can access Bitcoin-backed assets within Canton’s privacy-enabled ecosystem, supporting use cases including trading, lending and asset transfers. The asset incorporates distributed reserve controls and Chainlink Proof of Reserve to provide transparency into its Bitcoin backing.

“As institutional adoption of digital assets continues to evolve, providing access to emerging blockchain ecosystems through trusted trading infrastructure is increasingly important,” said David Olsson, Chief Commercial Officer of EDX Markets. “Our partnership with BitSafe expands the range of assets available to EDX participants while creating a new point of access to Bitcoin-backed value on Canton. This listing reflects our continued commitment to connecting clients with new opportunities across digital asset markets.”

The launch introduces an initial CBTC/USD spot market, with plans to add CBTC/USD perpetual contracts in the coming weeks and CBTC/BTC spot trading planned for a later stage. EDX also plans to accept Canton Coin as eligible collateral for CBTC perpetual trading. In addition, EDX and BitSafe will introduce a trading incentive program that includes zero trading fees for eligible CBTC trades, covered CBTC withdrawal fees and Canton Coin rewards based on eligible trading volume, subject to program terms.

“Bitcoin has tremendous potential beyond being held as a standalone asset, particularly as institutional financial activity expands across Canton,” said Aki Balogh, CEO of BitSafe. “CBTC enables firms to put Bitcoin-backed value to work across trading, lending and other financial applications, while maintaining transparency into the asset’s backing. Partnering with EDX establishes an important new access point for market participants and supports the continued growth of the CBTC ecosystem.”

Granite River Trading (GRT), a principal digital-asset trading firm, will support liquidity across EDX’s CBTC markets, beginning with CBTC/USD spot and extending to additional CBTC markets as they launch.

“Institutions want deep, reliable markets before they put Bitcoin to work on Canton,” said Josh Gibson, CEO and Co-Founder of GRT. “As a Canton validator and day-one liquidity partner on EDX, we’ll be quoting two-sided CBTC/USD markets from launch. Liquidity is what turns a new listing into a real market, and we’re glad to help BitSafe build it.”

The collaboration reflects EDX Markets’ and BitSafe’s shared commitment to expanding access to digital assets and supporting the growth of Canton’s financial ecosystem. By combining EDX’s trading infrastructure with BitSafe’s Bitcoin-backed asset, the firms aim to enhance liquidity, broaden market participation and create new opportunities for institutions to engage with Bitcoin-backed value on Canton.

item.title: CFTC Staff Addresses Use Of Trust Companies For Daily Settlements
item.content:encoded:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Clearing and Risk today issued a no-action letter addressing whether derivatives clearing organizations may use trust companies to conduct daily settlements with clearing members.

According to the letter, a derivatives clearing organization may use a trust company for daily settlements if it treats the trust company as it would a settlement bank under applicable CFTC requirements.

item.title: Nodal Exchange Achieves Strong Performance In All Markets In October 2026
item.content:encoded:
Nodal Exchange today announced strong performance in power, environmental, and natural gas futures in October 2026. Traded power futures on Nodal Exchange were 299.3 million MWh in October 2026, a 7% increase from the month prior. October was also the exchange’s second-highest month of power futures volume in 2026. Nodal is the #1 power futures exchange in the U.S. with 1.439 billion MWh of open interest and over 55% market share as of the end of October 2026.  The open interest represents the electricity to serve almost all of the approximately 134 million households in the United States for a year.

Environmental futures and options on Nodal Exchange posted volume of 68,535 lots in October, up slightly from a year earlier. Open interest ended the month at 494,389 lots, up 14% from a year earlier.

Renewable energy certificate (REC) futures and options posted volume of 32,256 lots in October and ended the month with open interest of 387,476 lots, up 28% from October 2025. Carbon futures and options across CCA, RGGI, WCA and Carbon Offsets products posted volume of 27,907 lots in October and ended the month with open interest of 81,249 lots.

Open interest in Nodal’s natural gas markets reached 7,500,000 MMBtus as of the end of October 2026, a 43% increase from a year ago.

“Nodal Exchange is proud to serve these markets, and we are very pleased to see them continue to grow,” said Paul Cusenza, Chairman and CEO of Nodal Exchange. “Managing risk in these markets is increasingly important, and we will continue to seek to best meet the evolving needs of the participants we serve.”

item.title: FINRA Fines Webull $4.2 Million For Anti-Money Laundering And Best Execution Violations - Firm Failed To Monitor For Suspicious Transactions, Reasonably Verify Customer Identities And Consider Execution Quality Available At Competing Markets
item.content:encoded:
FINRA has fined Webull Financial LLC $4.2 million for failing to implement reasonably designed programs for anti-money laundering (AML), identity theft prevention and best execution. FINRA also ordered Webull to certify remediation of the deficiencies in its AML and identity theft prevention programs and retain an independent consultant to address its best execution program. 

Webull experienced rapid and significant growth between January 2020 and September 2023, opening millions of new customer accounts each year. From at least February 2020, the firm executed billions of shares and received payment for order flow. 

“Webull’s business grew rapidly, but its compliance program did not keep pace,” said Bill St. Louis, Executive Vice President and Head of Enforcement at FINRA. “Firms must ensure that their supervisory systems grow with their business and address the risks they present. Webull failed to do so in fundamental areas, including verifying its customers’ identities, detecting suspicious activity and ensuring the best possible execution of customer trades. FINRA holds firms accountable when their compliance programs do not adequately address the risks created by their business.”

AML Violations

Between January 2020 and September 2023, Webull approved the opening of more than 120,000 new customer accounts using identity verification services provided by its third-party vendors without forming a reasonable belief that it knew the true identity of those customers. For example, the firm approved accounts for more than 50 customers who submitted photos of scenic landscapes instead of government-issued identification. In other instances, the firm approved accounts for customers despite information in the firm’s own systems indicating that the customers were deceased.

Fraud Prevention Failings

Over the same period, Webull failed to detect and report a variety of suspicious transactions. For example, Webull failed to identify or investigate 473 unauthorized ACH transfers used to transfer over $1.5 million from customers at other financial institutions into Webull accounts. It also failed to timely investigate a single account that triggered nearly 13,000 alerts for potentially manipulative trading activity in more than 100 stock symbols during the approximately 18 months the account was open. 

Additionally,Webull lacked several surveillance capabilities essential for identifying fraudulent activities occurring at the firm, undermining investor and market protections. The firm did not have any processes to identify potentially suspicious out-of-the-money options trading. The firm lacked surveillance to identify instances in which unrelated customers were trading from the same address or device. The firm also lacked reasonable surveillance to detect fraudulent account takeovers in a timely manner.

Between January 2020 and February 2023, Webull also failed to have an identity theft prevention program reasonably designed to detect, prevent and mitigate identity theft, instead relying on a deficient customer identification program. As a result, the firm failed to detect certain red flags associated with identity theft and opened dozens of accounts for foreign nationals using the same IP address or device. The firm also did not implement a process to check whether multiple unrelated accounts were opened using the same social security number until August 2021.

Best Execution Violations

FINRA also found that Webull failed to reasonably supervise for best execution and failed to conduct reasonable regular and rigorous reviews of customers’ execution quality. At certain points between at least February 2020 to at least May 2025, Webull conducted no review for the execution quality available at competing market centers and at other times obtained such data but failed to sufficiently review it. At certain points, the firm also failed to review execution quality for non-marketable orders—which made up 60% to 70% of its order flow during certain periods—and did not conduct reviews on a type-of-order or security-by-security basis as required. 

In settling this matter, Webull consented to the entry of FINRA's findings without admitting or denying the charges. In addition to the $4.2 million fine, Webull agreed to certify remediation of the deficiencies in its AML and identity theft prevention programs and retain an independent consultant to address its best execution program. In 2025, FINRA censured and fined Webull $1.6 million for failing to reasonably supervise and retain social media communications by individuals with a significant number of followers on social media (commonly known as “influencers”) that promoted the firm. This included statements that were not fair and balanced, or were promissory or exaggerated, among other claims. 

FINRA Regulatory Notice 19-18 provides guidance to member firms regarding suspicious activity monitoring and reporting obligations under FINRA Rule 3310 (Anti-Money Laundering Compliance Program), and FINRA provides additional guidance and compliance training on AML compliance obligations. FINRA Regulatory Notice 21-23 provides member firms with information concerning best execution obligations under FINRA Rule 5310 (Best Execution and Interpositioning) and payment for order flow. The 2026 FINRA Annual Regulatory Oversight Report includes additional information regarding FINRA's areas of concern related to AML and best execution and order routing practices.

FINRA makes available disciplinary actions and other information on its Disciplinary Actions Online database. In addition, FINRA publishes on its Monthly Disciplinary Actions page a summary of disciplinary actions against firms and individuals for violations of FINRA rules; federal securities laws, rules and regulations; and the rules of the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board. FINRA’s use of fine monies is limited to specific purposes set forth in its public Financial Guiding Principles, which are approved by its Board of Governors. FINRA publicly itemizes and discloses how it uses fine monies each year.

item.title: US Department Of Justice Launches Super Intelligence Task Force
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of Justice is announcing the formation of its Super Intelligence (SI) Task Force (DOJ-SITF). President Trump has made clear that “America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence,” and the Department will be a leader in safeguarding against malicious SI actors. 

Led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss, the DOJ-SITF will ensure that America's leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

“SI development will continue to be powered by American innovators,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The SI Task Force at the Department of Justice will facilitate our partnership with SI Force Chair Jay Clayton as we ensure critical SI technologies serve the American people and are not manipulated by bad actors at home or abroad. The Department of Justice will continue identifying and prosecuting individuals whose use of SI violates the law, including by maliciously targeting American taxpayers, critical U.S. infrastructure, or other aspects of our national security.”

“As technological capabilities evolve, the DOJ-SITF will advance the Department’s mission to make America safe,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. “Our comprehensive effort will promote innovation and prevent the misuse of Super Intelligence.”

“The creation of the DOJ-SITF marks an important moment for the Department to help advance SI technologies and, at the same time, protect American innovation," said Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss. "The Department also has a responsibility to utilize law enforcement tools at our disposal to deter improper use of SI, harden regular reporting on SI risk and response, and ensure companies exercise vigorous internal controls so that SI technology behaves as intended. The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests.”

The increase compared to Q3 2025 reflects investments in growth and the impact of Euronext Athens acquired in November 2025, in line with the underlying cost guidance for full-year 2026. Driven by the double-digit growth in revenue, adjusted EBITDA for the quarter reached €364.2 million, up +31.6% compared to Q3 2025. This represents a record adjusted EBITDA margin of 66.5%, up +3.3pts vs. Q3 2025. On a like-for-like basis at constant currencies, adjusted EBITDA grew by +23.2% compared to Q3 2025.

Euronext reported €8.4 million of non-underlying expenses in Q3 2026, mostly related to the integration of Euronext Athens, Admincontrol and GRSS. Q3 2026 reported EBITDA was at €355.8 million, up +29.3% compared to Q3 2025.

 

  • Q3 2026 net income, share of the parent company shareholders

     

Depreciation and amortisation accounted for €54.2 million in Q3 2026, +10.1% more than Q3 2025. PPA related to acquired businesses accounted for €24.3 million.

Adjusted operating profit was €340.0 million, up +34.1% compared to Q3 2025.

Euronext reported a net financing expense of €8.4 million in Q3 2026, compared to a €6.8 million net financing expense in Q3 2025. This difference resulted from higher financing expenses due to the new bond issuances with higher financing costs, and FX impacts.

Income tax for Q3 2026 was €77.5 million. This translated into an effective tax rate of 26.4% for the quarter, compared to 26.7% in Q3 2025.

Share of non-controlling interests amounted to €21.1 million, correlated with the strong performance of MTS, Euronext Athens and Nord Pool.

As a result, the reported net income, share of the parent company shareholders, increased by +30.2% for Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025, to €194.9 million. This represents a reported EPS of €1.92 basic and €1.90 diluted. Adjusted net income, share of the parent company shareholders, was up +32.0% to €223.2 million. Adjusted EPS was €2.21 basic and €2.17 diluted.

The weighted number of shares used over the third quarter of 2026 was 101,291,091 for the basic calculation and 103,777,362 for the diluted calculation, compared to 101,294,214 and 102,688,870 respectively over the third quarter of 2025. The difference is due to the share repurchase programme executed by Euronext, the share issuance for the acquisition of Euronext Athens and the impact of the convertible bonds on the diluted share count.

In Q3 2026, Euronext reported a net cash flow from operating activities of €208.2 million, compared to €401.0 million in Q3 2025, reflecting higher profit before tax, negative changes in working capital from CCP activities and higher income tax in Q3 2026. Excluding the impact on working capital from Euronext Clearing and Nord Pool CCP activities, net cash flow from operating activities accounted for 88.5% of EBITDA in Q3 2026.

Q3 2026 corporate highlights since publication of the second quarter 2026 results on 30 July 2026

 

  • Euronext announced the go-live of the new European CSD model

     

Euronext Securities' new European CSD model, live since 21 September, is a game changer for European capital markets. For the first time, market participants can choose between their domestic infrastructure or consolidating their activity within a single European framework. Euronext Securities is now the designated default CSD for equities and ETPs on Euronext Amsterdam, Brussels and Paris, building on a network already serving Athens, Copenhagen, Milan, Oslo and Porto.

This new service is a tangible step towards a more unified European capital market. By enabling clients to consolidate activity across multiple markets within a single account while benefitting from greater choice in post-trade services, Euronext helps reduce market fragmentation and improve operational efficiency. Leveraging its connection to TARGET2-Securities (T2S), Euronext delivers these benefits without diluting market liquidity, reinforcing the resilience and competitiveness of Europe’s market infrastructure. Additional clients can access the model through Euronext’s growing network of partners, including leading issuer agents and custodians. The first ever Belgian issuer moved to Euronext Securities in October 2026, and Euronext will support more Belgian issuers thanks to the newly formed partnership with KBC Securities Services.

  • Euronext announced the acquisition of the remaining 25% stake in GRSS

     

Following the acquisition of a 75% stake in June 2024, in August 2026 Euronext acquired the remaining 25% of Global Rate Set Systems (GRSS) and now owns 100% of the company's share capital. GRSS is a leading provider of services to benchmark administrators, helping them develop, calculate and distribute critical benchmarks to the financial markets. GRSS provides mission-critical services to the benchmark administrators of three of Europe’s most critical interest rate benchmarks: EURIBOR (global, the world’s largest benchmark), STIBOR (Sweden) and NIBOR (Norway). GRSS is also itself the benchmark administrator of the CIBOR and CITA (Denmark), PRIBOR (Czech Republic) and the TAB, TADO and ICP (Chile).

The successful acquisition and integration of GRSS is further proof of Euronext’s unmatched ability to successfully deploy critical market infrastructure to the benefit of European markets.

 

Corporate highlights since 1 October 2026

  • Expansion of the power franchise across Europe 

     

At the end of October, Nord Pool launched day-ahead power trading services in Slovenia, marking its entry into the 17th European market and further expanding presence in Central and Southeastern Europe. The launch follows the successful implementation of the Multi-NEMO Arrangement in Slovenia, giving local market participants greater choice in accessing day-ahead power trading services. This milestone strengthens Euronext’s position as a leading pan-European power market operator, contributes to the integration of European electricity markets and aligns with Euronext’s strategy to expand the physical and financial power franchise across Europe.

  • Euronext intends to nominate David Knibbe as Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Managing Board

     

On 2 November 2026, Euronext N.V. announced that, following the recommendation by the Nomination Committee, the Supervisory Board, chaired by Piero Novelli, intends to nominate David Knibbe as Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Managing Board of Euronext N.V. at the Annual General Meeting on 20 May 2027.

David Knibbe will join from NN Group N.V., where he has been CEO since 2019. He brings extensive experience in leading a highly regulated business, delivering operational transformations and substantial shareholder value creation, positioning him well to continue to scale Euronext through the next phase of strategic growth and further advance the integration of European capital markets. He will be based in Paris.

The nomination of David Knibbe follows Stéphane Boujnah’s decision to step down from his role in May 2027 and a thorough and diligent selection process conducted by the Supervisory Board, which considered several candidates in light of the Group’s strategic priorities and long-term ambitions.

The appointment of David Knibbe is subject to the approval by the relevant National Competent Authorities (NCAs), the Dutch Minister of Finance and will be submitted for approval by Euronext’s shareholders at the Annual General Meeting to be held on 20 May 2027.

item.title: Alberta Securities Commission: Former Investment Bank Employee And His Mother Pay $330,000 In Insider Trading Settlement
item.content:encoded:
The Alberta Securities Commission (ASC) has concluded a Settlement Agreement and Undertaking with Calgary residents Dean Labbe and his mother, Julie Labbe, for breaching Alberta securities laws through a multi-year insider trading scheme. Dean Labbe repeatedly used confidential information from his work at an investment bank to trade securities and recommend trades through accounts held in his mother's name.

Dean Labbe was employed at an investment bank between May 2018 and June 2024. He worked on mergers, acquisitions and other potential transactions for the bank's clients and regularly obtained confidential information about reporting issuers and proposed transactions.

Between December 2018 and March 2024, Dean Labbe purchased securities, or recommended to his mother that she purchase securities, in 10 Canadian issuers involved in transactions on which he or his colleagues were working. The purchases were made while Dean Labbe was in possession of material, non-public information about the issuers.

The trading activity generated profits of approximately $130,000. Seven of the 10 transactions involved acquisitions, and in each instance, securities of the target issuer were purchased before the acquisition was announced.

Dean Labbe used brokerage accounts held in his mother’s name rather than accounts in his own name and did not disclose the trading activity to his employer. Julie Labbe knew that Dean Labbe was using confidential information obtained through his employment to select or recommend securities, and permitted the use of her accounts. She also knew that the accounts were being used to conceal the purchases from his employer.
  
Dean Labbe admitted that he engaged in illegal insider trading and illegally recommended or encouraged Julie Labbe to purchase securities. Julie Labbe admitted that she authorized, permitted or acquiesced in Dean Labbe's insider trading by maintaining accounts for his use with knowledge of his conduct.

Under the terms of the Settlement Agreement and Undertaking:

  • Dean Labbe is prohibited from trading in or purchasing securities or derivatives for 20 years, subject to limited exceptions;
  • Julie Labbe is prohibited from trading in or purchasing securities or derivatives for 10 years, subject to limited exceptions; and
  • The Labbes paid a monetary settlement of $330,000 to the ASC, inclusive of costs.

"Dean Labbe was entrusted through his employment with highly confidential information about corporate transactions, and he repeatedly exploited that trust for personal gain," said Cynthia Campbell, Director of Enforcement at the ASC. "The 20-year trading ban reflects the need to protect Alberta investors and our capital markets from individuals who misuse material, non-public information. Fair and efficient markets depend on investor confidence that no one is trading with an unfair informational advantage."

The Settlement Agreement and Undertaking resolves the matters alleged in a Notice of Hearing issued October 15, 2025. As a result, the hearing into these allegations scheduled to begin December 1, 2026, will not proceed.

A copy of the Settlement Agreement and Undertaking is available on the ASC website at asc.ca.

The ASC is the regulatory agency responsible for administering the province’s securities laws. It is entrusted with fostering a fair and efficient capital market in Alberta and with protecting investors. As a member of the Canadian Securities Administrators, the ASC works to improve, coordinate and harmonize the regulation of Canada’s capital markets.

item.title: Corporate CUSIP Request Volumes Rise In October - Municipal Volumes Edge Higher
item.content:encoded:
CUSIP Global Services (CGS) today announced the release of its CUSIP Issuance Trends Report for October 2026. The report, which tracks the issuance of new security identifiers as an early indicator of debt and capital markets activity over the next quarter, found a monthly increase in request volume for new corporate identifiers, and a modest increase in request volume for new municipal identifiers.

North American corporate CUSIP requests totaled 9,714 in October, which represents a 6.7% increase on a monthly basis. On an annualized basis, North American corporate requests were up 11.1% over October 2025 totals. Requests for new U.S. corporate debt identifiers rose 11.9% and requests for new U.S. corporate equity identifiers fell 11.4% for the month of October.

The aggregate total of identifier requests for new municipal securities – including municipal bonds, long-term and short-term notes, and commercial paper – rose 1.8% versus September totals. On a year-over-year basis, overall municipal volumes were down 1.1% through the end of October. Texas led state-level municipal request volume with a total of 181 new CUSIP requests in October, followed by New York (123) and California (93).

“Corporate request volume rose for a second straight month in October, led by a double-digit increase in new U.S. corporate debt identifiers,” said Gerard Faulkner, Director of Operations for CGS. “Private placement requests also climbed sharply from September, and municipal volumes were higher for a third consecutive month, all of which are strong indications of healthy new security issuance activity as we head into the final quarter of 2026.”

Requests for international equity CUSIPs fell 8.5% in October and international debt CUSIP requests were down 18.8%. On an annualized basis, international equity CUSIP requests were down 1.7% and international debt CUSIP requests were up 10.7%.

item.title: Shaping The Future Of Money, Keynote Speech By Piero Cipollone, Member Of The Executive Board Of The ECB, At The Eighth International Conference Of Regional Card Schemes And Retail Financial Market Infrastructures, Tirana, 5 November 2026
item.content:encoded:
Money connects people and societies.

But to do this, it must be trusted. It must allow people and businesses to transact safely and efficiently. And it must evolve with geopolitical and technological developments.

For centuries, central banks have issued money and safeguarded its value. That mandate remains unchanged. But the environment in which money is used is being transformed.

People are increasingly paying digitally. Tokenisation could reorganise the financial value chain. New solutions are being considered to enhance cross-border payments. And geopolitical fragmentation is making the resilience and governance of critical infrastructure ever more important.

Central banks must therefore ensure that the money they issue remains fit for the future.

This does not mean replacing the private sector or predicting which technology will prevail. It means providing a trusted public foundation for payments and finance on which private innovation can flourish. And it means preventing digitalisation from increasing fragmentation or creating new dependencies.

This is why the Eurosystem has adopted a comprehensive payments strategy.[1]

The strategy has four objectives: ensuring that central bank money can continue to settle retail and wholesale transactions as preferences and technologies evolve; strengthening Europe’s resilience and strategic autonomy; fostering an integrated, competitive and innovative payments ecosystem; and supporting the international role of the euro.

In other words, we are seeking to comprehensively upgrade money and payments in Europe.

The Western Balkans are also taking active policy steps to enhance and integrate payments in the region. Several countries, including Albania, have already joined the Single Euro Payments Area. And a clone of the Eurosystem’s fast payment system (TIPS), developed by Banca d’Italia, is already fully operational in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro and will soon be launched in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia. It allows real-time, low-cost domestic transactions in local currencies around the clock, every day of the year.

This represents real, tangible progress that people will benefit from in their daily lives.

But we must always think one step ahead.

So today, I will discuss four key initiatives we are working on.

We are modernising euro banknotes.

We are developing a digital euro.

We are making it possible to settle tokenised asset transactions in central bank money and creating the conditions for an integrated and innovative tokenised finance ecosystem.

And we are interlinking fast payment systems to make cross-border payments faster and more efficient.

These initiatives have a common goal: ensuring access to safe public money while creating space for private innovation and international cooperation.

Modernising euro banknotes

Let me begin with the most familiar form of central bank money: cash.

In discussions about digitalisation, cash is sometimes talked about as a technology of the past. That is a mistake. In an age where cyber risks, hybrid threats and system outages make the headlines, cash remains the most resilient form of payment we have.

More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation. People do not just see cash as a means of payment; they also view it as a store of value and a safeguard in periods of uncertainty. And it is one of the most tangible symbols of European unity.

Moreover, cash is inclusive and simple to use, as it does not require a device or an intermediary. It protects privacy. And, most importantly, it gives people freedom of choice.

That is why Europe is not choosing between cash and digital payments. We are investing in both.

The Single Currency Package reflects this approach.[2] Alongside the proposed Regulation on the establishment of a digital euro, it includes a proposed Regulation on the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins. The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have adopted their respective positions, and the interinstitutional negotiations are under way.

But protecting cash is not enough. We must also prepare it for the future.

The next generation of euro banknotes will incorporate enhanced security features, have a smaller environmental impact and improve accessibility. We also want Europeans to feel that their banknotes reflect the cultural identity and natural environment they share.

This summer, almost ten million people shared their views in a public survey on the ten shortlisted design proposals. Two-thirds of the responses came from people under the age of 35.[3]

This remarkable level of participation shows that Europeans continue to care deeply about their banknotes.

The ECB’s Governing Council expects to decide on the final design concept around the end of this year. The future euro banknotes should enter circulation gradually from the early 2030s, while existing banknotes will remain valid.

So the future of public money will remain physical.

But it must also be digital.

Preparing a future-ready digital euro

Today, central bank money is only available to the public as cash. But physical cash cannot be used online or for the ever-growing range of digital transactions.

Europe also lacks a digital solution that can be used for everyday payments across the euro area. Digital payments remain fragmented along national lines and use cases. And we have a strategic dependency: 13 euro area countries rely entirely on non-European companies for in-store card payments.

The digital euro would remedy this situation.

It would be a digital form of cash issued by the Eurosystem, available and accepted throughout the euro area. It would complement banknotes and coins, not replace them. It could be used in shops, online and between individuals.

It would work both online and offline. Basic use would be free for consumers. And we are designing it to provide high levels of security, privacy, accessibility and resilience.

The offline functionality would allow payments to be made without an internet connection. It would also offer cash-like privacy, as the personal transaction details would be known only to the payer and payee. For online transactions, the Eurosystem would not know the individuals involved in the payment.

The digital euro would therefore preserve people’s freedom to pay with central bank money as the economy becomes more digital.

But it would do more than provide another payment option.

It would create a common public infrastructure and acceptance layer for European payments. Payment service providers could build on that infrastructure and use the digital euro’s open standards to offer services throughout the euro area.

The digital euro would help private European payment solutions expand beyond their current geographical and functional boundaries. It would lower investment costs and allow providers to focus investment on customer-facing innovation.

And beyond the euro area, the digital euro standards and rulebook could provide a useful blueprint for countries that are considering developing a domestic scheme for digital payments. This would facilitate interoperability with the digital euro in the future.

The objective of the digital euro is not to displace private payment solutions. On the contrary, it will provide a common foundation on which the private sector can compete, innovate and achieve European scale.

Banks and other supervised payment service providers would remain the main point of contact for users. They would distribute the digital euro and provide customer services. The Eurosystem would not charge scheme or processing fees. This will generate savings for banks, merchants – especially small ones – and ultimately consumers.

We are also designing safeguards to ensure that the digital euro functions as a means of payment rather than a form of investment. It would not be remunerated, and individual holdings would be limited. But this would not restrict transactions: a waterfall system with a linked bank account would ensure that amounts above the holding limit can be sent or received.

Where the project stands

The legislative process is advancing. The Council of the EU agreed its position in December 2025, the European Parliament adopted its position in July 2026 and the trilogue negotiations are now under way. The European Council has called for the negotiations to be concluded by the end of this year. Assuming the legislative process is concluded by the end of 2026, we aim to be ready for a potential first issuance in 2029.

But technical preparations must advance in parallel.

The digital euro pilot is planned to start in the second half of 2027 and will run for 12 months. We have selected 36 payment service providers from across the euro area following a call that attracted more than 50 applications.[4] Preparatory work is well under way.

The objective is not simply to test technology. A payments system is an ecosystem comprising service providers, merchants, central banks, infrastructure operators and users. The pilot will allow the members of this ecosystem to test the design of the digital euro, learn from experience and identify improvements.

On 15 September we launched a call inviting e-commerce and mobile-commerce merchants to take part in the pilot. The selected merchants will test customer payment journeys, assess integration with existing checkout systems and provide feedback on the user experience.[5]

The digital euro is not merely a fix for existing shortcomings in the euro area payments landscape. It is a solution for the future. It will provide a platform to innovate and enhance the quality and breadth of payment services. New opportunities are arising. We want to make sure that European payment service providers are in the best position to seize them and gain a strong competitive edge.

Against this backdrop, we recently launched a new wave of activities through the digital euro innovation platform, building on a first wave that involved around 70 market participants.[6]

One workstream will experiment with integrated electronic receipts, payments involving multiple payers or recipients, conditional payments and new features offered through payment apps.

A second workstream will look further ahead, exploring developments that could enhance the digital euro in future releases. This includes possible applications of artificial intelligence, such as AI agent-enabled payments or micropayments, and possible uses of a digital euro in interactions with public services, for example when paying for transportation, mobility and parking services.

We cannot know precisely how Europeans will want to pay 20 years from now. But we can build a foundation that is open to innovation, robust enough to earn public trust and able to evolve with users’ needs.

Pontes and Appia: supporting tokenised finance

Our third initiative concerns digital finance.

By allowing assets to be represented as digital files, tokenisation could change how they are issued, traded, settled, held and serviced.

Today, these activities often take place across separate infrastructures and ledgers. Tokenisation could bring them into a shared digital environment, allowing smart contracts to automate processes and generating efficiency gains that could reduce costs and lower the barriers for smaller firms to access finance.

But market participants have been clear that tokenised finance needs a safe settlement asset. Private instruments such as stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits can play useful roles. But central bank money provides risk-free final settlement and a common reference that private forms of money can be converted into at par. It ensures that one euro remains one euro, no matter its issuer, form or underlying technology.

Pontes: an operational bridge

The Eurosystem launched Pontes on 21 September.

Pontes connects market distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms with the Eurosystem’s TARGET Services, enabling wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money.

It builds on the Eurosystem’s exploratory work in 2024, in which 64 participants conducted more than 50 trials and experiments and settled almost €1.6 billion in central bank money. That work demonstrated the feasibility of central bank money settlement for DLT-based transactions and confirmed strong market demand for a risk-free settlement asset.

Pontes is now live with an initial group of market participants and DLT operators. On Monday, Pontes settled a €1 billion transaction in benchmark bonds successfully issued on DLT by the European Stability Mechanism.[7] Many other national and supernational institutions, including the World Bank, are preparing to issue on DLT and possibly settle in Pontes. Current Pontes services will be expanded gradually, with enhanced features, such as immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform and longer operating hours, being introduced as we move towards 24/7/365 availability in 2028.

Pontes provides a dependable settlement foundation for tokenised securities and helps connect private tokenised settlement assets to central bank money.

Appia: designing an integrated ecosystem

With tokenisation, we have an opportunity to create an integrated market for digital assets from the outset, which would help address the fragmentation of Europe’s capital markets. But technology does not guarantee integration. It could instead produce incompatible platforms, closed networks and fragmented pools of assets and liquidity.

For assets and services to interact across platforms, common standards are needed. Liquidity and collateral must be able to move. And the legal framework must provide clarity on issues such as ownership, settlement finality, custody and smart contracts.

That is why we launched our Appia project.

Appia addresses the architecture, standards and governance of a European tokenised financial ecosystem. It combines analysis, experimentation and public-private cooperation with the aim of delivering a blueprint in 2028.[8]

The market is actively contributing to this work. The public consultation on the Appia roadmap received 127 responses, and 90% of respondents made at least one proposal to contribute.[9]

Pontes and Appia are therefore two parts of one strategy.

Pontes provides a bridge that makes it possible to settle DLT-based transactions in central bank money, while Appia is designing the digital finance ecosystem of tomorrow.

Interlinking fast payment systems

Our fourth initiative concerns cross-border payments.

Domestic payments have become dramatically faster. Yet international payments often remain slow, expensive and opaque. High costs reduce the value of remittances. And long payment chains complicate trade, particularly for smaller businesses.

Our approach is to connect the fast payment systems that central banks and the private sector have already built. This will help lower the cost of payments and make them faster.

TIPS, the Eurosystem’s instant payment settlement service, settles payments in central bank money around the clock. It already supports the euro, the Swedish krona and the Danish krone, with the Norwegian krone and Icelandic króna set to join in the coming years. Its cross-currency service has been available since October 2025.

In July the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Central Bank of Montenegro successfully launched a platform for the settlement of instant payments, which uses TIPS technology. The number of transactions is increasing each day: on Monday it was already close to 30,000 transactions per day. Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia are expected to join soon, bringing all countries participating in the initiative onto the platform. This will help to modernise payments in the region and support its integration.

We are now working to connect TIPS with payment systems globally.

Interlinking enables fast payment systems to communicate. People can continue using their existing bank and payment arrangements, while transfers reach beneficiaries connected to another jurisdiction’s system.

This can shorten payment chains and reduce costs. It also respects monetary sovereignty because participating jurisdictions retain control of their currencies and domestic infrastructures.

Interlinking therefore offers a practical model of international cooperation: strengthening connections without surrendering sovereignty.

Work is advancing on a bilateral link with India’s Unified Payments Interface, the largest fast payment system in the world by transaction volume. We are also examining a potential connection to Nexus Global Payments, which will connect fast payment systems in South-East Asia, and exploring links with the instant payment systems of Switzerland and Brazil. Last week, the leaders of EU and Canada also indicated that they would support work towards connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower-cost and more seamless transactions across the two economies.[10]

As for the Western Balkans, at least two tracks can be envisaged: the first and most straightforward is full integration in the EU. In that case the reference model would be Sweden and Denmark until the eventual adoption of euro. The alternative would be exploring possible interlinking with TIPS, once the business case justifies the investment. In any case, the TIPS clone should by its very nature already support integration, as payment services providers operating in both the euro area and the Western Balkans will be using two platforms that are technically very similar. This would make it easier for them to provide traditional correspondent banking services.

Conclusion

Let me conclude.

The four initiatives I have presented today are different dimensions of the same transformation. We are making sure that central bank money remains fit for purpose as preferences, technologies and the geopolitical landscape evolve.

Modernising banknotes ensures that public money remains tangible, inclusive and resilient.

The digital euro would make public money available for digital payments and create a European infrastructure that private payment service providers can use as a platform for innovation.

Pontes and Appia ensure that central bank money remains the settlement anchor as financial markets adopt tokenisation.

And interlinking fast payment systems connects jurisdictions while respecting their monetary sovereignty.

The future of money will not be defined by a single instrument or a single technology. It will involve physical and digital money, public and private solutions, and domestic and cross-border infrastructures. It will be shaped by the choices we make about trust, openness, resilience and sovereignty. These choices will determine whether Europe can once again be a cradle of monetary innovation.

Our responsibility as central banks is to ensure that these elements form a coherent, trusted and resilient monetary system.

We cannot merely observe the transformation of money from the sidelines. We have a duty to shape it in the public interest.

Thank you.

  1. ECB (2026), The Eurosystem's comprehensive payments strategy.

  2. European Commission (2023), “Single Currency Package: new proposals to support the use of cash and to propose a framework for a digital euro”, press release, 28 June.

  3. ECB (2026), “Almost ten million people took part in ECB survey on new euro banknotes”, press release, 23 September.

  4. See ECB (2026), “ECB selects 36 payment service providers to join digital euro pilot”, press release, 14 July and the digital euro pilot web page.

  5. See ECB (2026), “Call for online and mobile merchants to participate in digital euro pilot now open”, MIP news, 15 September.

  6. See ECB (2026), “Call for expressions of interest in a new wave of digital euro innovation platform activities”, MIP news, 28 September.

  7. European Stability Mechanism (2026), “ESM raises €1 billion with sale of first digitally native bond”, press release, 26 October.

  8. ECB (2026), Appia – paving the way for a future-ready, integrated financial ecosystem leveraging tokenisation and DLT, 11 March.

  9. ECB (2026), Eurosystem report on the public consultation on the Appia Roadmap, 28 October.

  10. Council of the European Union (2026), EU-Canada Summit 2026 Joint Statement – Building together an Alliance for the Future, 30 October.

item.title: Without Exchanges, Can Best Execution Survive? WFE Warns That Too Much Bilateral Trading Weakens Price Formation And Investor Protection
item.content:encoded:
The World Federation of Exchanges (WFE), the global industry association for exchanges and central counterparties (CCPs), today called for greater attention to the role of exchanges in investor protection as trading becomes increasingly fragmented across very different types of trade execution. 

In two new papers, To Serve and Protect and When is Liquidity?, the WFE sets out why investor protection depends on good market design, which makes it possible to enforce the crucial rules that apply to financial intermediaries. 

The papers look particularly at the effect of trading moving away from multilateral markets towards bilateral execution and the implications for liquidity and price formation.  

The WFE says policymakers need to look beyond headline trading volumes and consider how much liquidity is genuinely available to investors and whether this fragmentation is affecting the robust price formation that is essential for public confidence. 

The When is Liquidity? paper shows how headline volumes can give a misleading picture of the liquidity available at any given point in the trading day. Multilateral exchanges bring participants together, reduce the cost of finding a counterparty and support transparent price discovery. 

Fragmentation can make it harder for market makers to manage the risks of providing liquidity. They may be undermined by non-public, bilateral trading and phantom liquidity when providing prices on-exchange – a process which can ultimately reduce the liquidity available to investors and weaken price formation. 

This matters for best execution. If it is difficult to establish where liquidity is genuinely available, it becomes harder to determine what the best possible execution price is. The WFE says policymakers should therefore consider how market design can serve investors, focusing on market depth on multilateral markets at any given point in time rather total trading volume. 

The papers also consider newer types of markets and assets, including crypto, prediction markets and carbon credits. The WFE says markets offering new ways of trading or new types of assets should be able to demonstrate how they support investor protection and meet the standards expected of regulated exchanges. 

Richard Metcalfe, Head of Regulatory Affairs at the WFE, said: “Investor protection starts with good market design. Exchanges provide the structure in which prices are formed, trading is governed by clear rules and market activity can be monitored. 

“As more trading moves into bilateral markets, we need to be clear about what that means for liquidity and price formation. If liquidity is not genuinely available, it becomes harder to know what the best execution price really is. That is a market structure issue, not simply a question of where an individual trade takes place.” 

Nandini Sukumar, Chief Executive Officer of the WFE, said: “Exchanges provide an important public reference point for financial markets. They help investors understand where prices are being formed and give companies a trusted market in which to raise capital. 

“Innovation has an important place in financial markets, but new forms of trading should not mean lower standards for investors. If a market is providing a different route to trading, it should be able to demonstrate that it provides the same level of investor protection and market integrity.”

  • Read in full: To Serve and Protect: Exchanges and Investor Protection  
  • Read in full: When is Liquidity? Investor Protection and the Way Share Trading Functions

item.title: Coinshares Comment: Bitcoin Takes The Democratic Sweep In Its Stride As Rates Stay In Charge
item.content:encoded:
James Butterfill, Head of Research at CoinShares

“Democratic control of Congress puts CLARITY on a harder path. With stablecoin law already passed and regulators moving on their own, a Fed priced for a December hike remains the bigger test for Bitcoin. 

Bitcoin has taken the Democratic sweep remarkably calmly, which is perhaps unsurprising given markets had been rehearsing the outcome for weeks. Democrats have now secured both the House and Senate, materially constraining Trump for the remaining two years of his presidency. But much of that was already in the price. The more interesting question is whether Trump becomes a lame duck or something rather less predictable. He retains considerable authority over foreign policy, trade and executive action, so less ability to legislate does not necessarily mean less ability to move markets.

For crypto, the immediate casualty is likely to be the speed of legislation rather than the direction of travel. CLARITY now faces a considerably harder path, and Democratic control gives the party greater influence over committee agendas, appointments and investigations into Trump-linked crypto ventures. That could produce some uncomfortable headlines. But CLARITY is also becoming less important than it was a year ago. GENIUS is already law, while the SEC and CFTC have moved ahead with rulemaking and exemptions of their own, including measures around tokenised securities and market structure. In other words, Congress is no longer the only route to regulatory progress. CLARITY would still provide more durable statutory certainty, particularly for Ether, DeFi and token issuers, but its absence is no longer synonymous with regulatory paralysis.

The consequences should also differ markedly across the market. Bitcoin is relatively insulated from the legislative wrangling because its regulatory status is already well established. US exchanges, token issuers and businesses dependent on new permissions have considerably more at stake. The same scrutiny could even strengthen established compliant operators by raising the cost of doing business for weaker competitors. Among listed crypto equities, miners with power, land and operating data centres remain particularly interesting as AI hyperscalers compete for infrastructure that cannot be built overnight.

Politics aside, Bitcoin still appears to be taking most of its instruction from rates, liquidity and institutional flows. Oil has fallen sharply this week as tentative progress in US-Iran talks reduced fears of another escalation. That takes some pressure off the inflation outlook and, if sustained, should give the Fed a little more room than it appeared to have only a fortnight ago.

The US economy, however, continues to be inconveniently resilient. September job openings rose to 7.5M, while ADP employment came in at 86k against expectations of 67k. Recent PMI data have also pointed to strong activity, with the October flash composite consistent with robust growth. Friday’s payroll report is therefore the next test. Consensus around 65k looks rather pessimistic to us, with some of the better survey indicators pointing closer to 100k.

Even a reasonably strong payroll number may not alter the December debate very much, with another 25bp hike already heavily priced.  There is therefore a slightly odd combination emerging. The election probably slows crypto legislation, but removes an important source of political uncertainty. Falling oil improves the inflation picture, while strong activity stops the Fed becoming comfortably dovish.

For Bitcoin, that leaves the medium-term outlook broadly unchanged. The election itself was never the dominant variable. Real yields, dollar liquidity and ETP demand remain more important, while the reduced importance of CLARITY means the legislative setback should be felt more acutely in the broader crypto complex than in Bitcoin itself.”

item.title: Signicat Climbs Financial Times & Statista’s Europe’s Long-Term Growth Champions Ranking For Third Consecutive Year - Signicat Rises To 76th Place After Over A Decade Of Sustained Growth
item.content:encoded:
Signicat, the leading European Digital Identity platform, has been named one of the Financial Times and Statista’s Europe’s Long-Term Growth Champions 2027, marking its third consecutive appearance in the ranking. The ranking recognises companies that have sustained primarily organic revenue growth over ten years.

“Three consecutive appearances are a great achievement on this prestigious list ,” said Asger Hattel, CEO of Signicat. “Our growth has been sustained over a decade because we have consistently expanded our market share by building a platform that our customers fundamentally trust. “Whether you pay taxes in Spain, go to the doctor in France, travel into the UK from Europe, check your bank account in Sweden or Norway, return bottles for recycling in Netherlands or use your digital ID wallet in Denmark, Signicat’s technology is being used”, he concludes.

item.title: Dubai Future Finance Week Day Four: Events Chart The Path For The Future Of Family Wealth And Tokenised Finance
item.content:encoded:
• Dubai Family Wealth Summit advances succession, governance and responsible stewardship, marking the UAE’s Year of Family
  • DIFC announces 2027 NextGen Internship programme to equip future family-enterprise leaders with practical industry experience
  • Future Tokenisation Forum considers how tokenised finance can move beyond fragmented use cases towards trusted, scalable market infrastructure 
  • DIFC Courts and DFSA tokenisation publications identify foundations required to support trusted, scalable and internationally connected tokenised market
  • Investment Leaders Exchange convenes sovereign wealth funds, institutional leaders, and family office principals to align long-term asset allocation across traditional and digital assets

Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), the leading global financial centre in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia (MEASA) region, focused on two connected but distinct shifts shaping long-term capital on day four of the inaugural Dubai Future Finance Week(Opens in a new tab). 

Held under the directives and patronage of His Highness Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance of the UAE, and President of DIFC, day four explored how family wealth and enterprises are preserved across generations, and how trusted infrastructure can support the issuance, ownership, settlement and distribution of tokenised assets.


The future of family wealth
 
The Dubai Family Wealth Summit addressed priorities for family businesses, family offices, ultra-high-net-worth principals and next-generation stewards. The focus of the event included governance and succession; wealth structuring and investment amid regulatory and geoeconomic change; technology and future assets; and responsible capital, philanthropy, impact and resilience. The Summit reflected a broader view of family wealth: continuity is not solely centred on asset management, but also depends on leadership, family unity, jurisdictional resilience and the future of family enterprises. The event underscored the growing importance of structured succession, effective governance and responsible capital stewardship. 
 
His Excellency Dr. Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, UAE Minister of Foreign Trade, delivered a keynote address during The Dubai Family Wealth Summit, reinforcing the importance of international connectivity and collaboration as Dubai continues to strengthen its position as a global hub for trade, investment and financial services.

Key speakers included Hussain Sajwani, Chairman, DAMAC Group; Halima Dangote, GED Family Office & International Offices, Dangote Industries Limited; Maurice Gravier, Group Chief Investment Officer for Wealth Management, Emirates NBD; Shehab Gargash, Founder, Gargash Prime; and Osama Ibrahim Seddiqi, Vice Chairman, Seddiqi Holding. 

As part of the Summit, DIFC announced a 2027 internship programme for the next-generation of leaders preparing to take on roles in family businesses. Building on the success of this year’s inaugural NextGen leadership programme, the internships will place participants in DIFC firms, providing practical experience across financial services, auditing, consultancy, law, support services, and AI, FinTech and innovation. The 2027 NextGen Internship Programme responds to an estimated USD 18.3trn in wealth estimated to be transferred globally by 2030 and sets out how Dubai is preparing the next generation to govern, invest and transfer family wealth.

 
A tokenised future
 
The Future Tokenisation Forum was opened by Mark Steward, Chief Executive of the DFSA and the event brought together regulators, financial institutions, investors and technology providers to consider how tokenised finance can move beyond fragmented use cases towards trusted, scalable market infrastructure. 

Sessions examined digital settlement mechanisms, programmable infrastructure, institutional custody, regulatory compliance, legal certainty, and cross-border interoperability. The discussions also examined how traditional finance, digital assets and Web3 infrastructure can work together, and what is needed for institutional adoption at scale. 

At the forum, the DFSA shared insights from their upcoming publications on tokenisation, highlighting the regulatory, legal and operational considerations shaping the evolution of digital finance. The report explored the foundations required to support trusted, scalable and internationally connected tokenised markets, while addressing key opportunities and challenges associated with wider adoption.
 
Mark Steward, Chief Executive of the DFSA, said: “Our new DFSA report, Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead, brings together perspectives and insights from leading market practitioners across the financial services ecosystem. As tokenisation moves into live use across financial products, payments, and market infrastructure, important questions about what is needed for tokenised markets to thrive and achieve scale responsibly need to be addressed. We hope this white paper will stimulate further discussion among industry, investors, regulators, and policymakers about the road ahead.”
 
The Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA) published its new report, Scaling Tokenisation: The Road Ahead, bringing together perspectives from leading practitioners across the financial services ecosystem, including BlackRock, Ripple, Robinhood, Soter Insure and Standard Chartered. The paper examines how tokenisation may develop as it moves from experimentation towards practical use across financial products, payments, and market infrastructure, and considers the conditions that may support its responsible development at scale. 

The report does not predict a single path for tokenisation or prescribe a particular technological, regulatory, or commercial outcome. Instead, it highlights areas of broad agreement and differing market views, and seeks to convene further discussion among industry, investors, regulators, policymakers, and international standard-setters. It also places that discussion in the context of DIFC’s internationally connected financial community and the development of trusted, connected, and scalable tokenised markets. 

Contributing to the broader discussion on tokenisation, the DIFC Courts, in collaboration with the DIFC Innovation Hub, DECA4 Advisory and industry partners, published a white paper proposing a new global standard for resolving disputes in the on-chain economy. At its centre is the Dispute Resolution Oracle (DRO) — an opt-in connection between smart contracts built on the blockchain/Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) and a trusted court or other qualifying chosen forum. The proposal addresses a critical gap in digital markets: while legal authorities can determine who is entitled to an asset, they cannot currently make that decision effective directly on-chain. The standard would allow parties to choose their forum before transacting, preserve the disputed asset when a claim is raised and once a final decision is reached then it can be fully enforced on chain.  

The initiative is designed as an open standard rather than a single jurisdiction solution. Human judges, arbitrators, mediators and experts would continue to decide cases off-chain, with safeguards including limited asset freezes, early review, reasoned decisions and appeal rights. 
 
Speakers included Glen Fernandes, Senior Executive Officer, DIFC Branch, BNY Mellon; Paul Kayrouz, Chief Fintech Officer, Central Bank of the UAE; William Mason, Director General, Guernsey Financial Services Commission; Amna Al Owais, Deputy Director of DIFC Courts; Michail Fekkas, First Vice Chairman, Hellenic Capital Market Commission; His Excellency Senator Osita Izunaso, Chairman, Senate Committee on Capital Markets, Federal Republic of Nigeria;; and Ruben Bombardi, General Counsel and Head of Regulatory Enablement, and Paul Boots, Senior Director – Head of Sector Development, Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA).Also on day four, the Investment Leaders Exchange convened sovereign wealth funds, institutional capital allocators, and family office principals. The exchange facilitated strategic dialogues on asset allocation, cross-border risk management, and the integration of digital assets into multi-generational institutional portfolios.

Lianlian DigiTech (02598.HK), a leading global payment and FinTech platform, today announced the official opening of its Middle East regional office located in Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), the leading global financial centre in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia region. Building on the company’s earlier milestone of securing a Category 3D Payment Service Provider licence from the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), the opening marks the next phase of Lianlian DigiTech’s Middle East strategy, as it expands its cross-border payment and treasury capabilities from DIFC.
 
Established within DIFC, the company looks forward to fostering a collaborative partnership aimed at shared growth. This brings together DIFC's world-class financial infrastructure with Lianlian DigiTech's global network and localised expertise to deliver seamless cross-border payment and comprehensive treasury management solutions, supporting businesses operating between China, the Middle East and global markets.
 
His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer, DIFC Authority, said: “Dubai’s position as a global gateway for trade and investment continues to create significant opportunities for financial services companies connecting businesses across key international markets. Lianlian DigiTech’s expansion from DIFC reflects the strength of our ecosystem as a platform for companies seeking to scale across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia, while strengthening connectivity with Asia. Its growing capabilities in cross-border payments and treasury solutions will contribute to the financial infrastructure supporting businesses between China and the region, further reinforcing Dubai and DIFC’s role in enabling the future of global finance.”
 
Strengthening local capabilities through DIFC
 
Driven by the surging trade momentum across the China-UAE economic corridor, globalising enterprises increasingly demand agile localised collection, multi-currency cash management, and cross-border vendor payout capabilities. Navigating multi-jurisdictional compliance while enhancing capital liquidity has become a core priority for businesses expanding internationally.
 
Operating from DIFC’s dynamic financial ecosystem, Lianlian DigiTech will further deepen strategic synergies with regional banks, tier-one financial institutions, and commercial partners. Designed to address complex operational scenarios, the company’s localised offerings including cross-border collections, FX hedging/conversions, and global vendor disbursements will be delivered in strict accordance with relevant regulatory authorisations and licensing frameworks.
 
Supporting trade through treasury and capital efficiency
 
Addressing challenges including lengthy fund turnover cycles, multi-currency exchange costs and complex cross-border payment workflows, Lianlian DigiTech provides an integrated solution spanning local collections, FX conversions and global vendor disbursements. The company’s capabilities are designed to streamline payment and settlement processes, enhance treasury transparency and improve operational efficiency for businesses operating across international markets.
Furthermore, Lianlian DigiTech continues to consolidate its commercial ecosystem footprint in the Middle East. Building on its established partnership with regional e-commerce giant Noon, as well as supporting merchant settlements on major marketplaces like Amazon UAE and Amazon Saudi Arabia, Lianlian DigiTech provides cross-border sellers with reliable revenue repatriation and multi-currency capital liquidity. The company remains dedicated to expanding scenario-based solutions to support corporate growth across the Middle East and globally.

Advancing China-GCC connectivity and regional growth
 
Positioned at the crossroads of global trade, Dubai serves as a vital commercial gateway connecting the Middle East, Africa, South Asia, and broader global markets. Under the ambitious Dubai Economic Agenda (D33) which aims to double the emirate's economy and drive foreign trade to AED 25.6 trillion over the next decade the accelerating economic ties between China and the UAE present unprecedented opportunities for digital financial infrastructure.
Lianlian DigiTech will continue to anchor its localisation strategy in the Middle East, expanding strategic alliances across regional institutions and commercial platforms. By combining its proprietary global payment architecture with deep localised insights, the company is positioned to support regional trade development and the continued international expansion of enterprises.

item.title: JPX Market Innovation & Research, Inc. Makes Strategic Investment In Smartround, Inc.
item.content:encoded:
JPX Market Innovation & Research, Inc. (JPXI) has made a strategic investment of approximately JPY 300 million in Smartround, Inc. (Smartround) through a combination of newly issued warrants and a secondary purchase of shares from an existing shareholder. The two companies have also signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to explore collaboration in three areas: (1) improving liquidity in Japan's private markets; (2) integrating Smartround's private-market data infrastructure with JPX Group's market infrastructure; and (3) delivering information and resources to startups, their shareholders, and investors.

Investment Rationale

JPXI, its parent company Japan Exchange Group, Inc., and its subsidiaries (collectively, JPX Group) are committed to contributing to realizing an affluent society through sustainable market development, including by improving the convenience of financial and capital markets.

Japan's ecosystem for pre-IPO and newly public companies and their investors faces two structural challenges: expanding access to growth capital for startups and enabling capital recycling for investors. The Study Group on Developing the Growth Market, established by Tokyo Stock Exchange, Inc., has identified the lack of liquidity for pre-IPO startup shares (private shares) as one of the issues that must be addressed to enable high growth after listing on the Growth Market.

Against this backdrop, Smartround operates smartround, an equity management platform for startups and investors covering cap table management, shareholder registry, stock option plan administration, and portfolio management. On October 2, 2026, building on this platform, Smartround launched its secondary offering service, SPO (Secondary Private Offering), which enables startups to run company-led / structured secondary transactions as part of their growth strategy through Smartround Securities, Inc. (Smartround Securities), its registered broker-dealer subsidiary. SPO enables startups to run structured secondary transactions* as part of their growth strategy.

(Note)
  • ･Transactions in which existing shareholders sell their private shares to new investors (private-market secondaries).

Through this investment, JPXI will support the development of secondary-market infrastructure for private shares and work to strengthen Japan's ecosystem for pre-IPO and newly public companies and their investors.

Areas of Potential Collaboration

The two companies will focus their discussions on the following three areas and work toward concrete initiatives.

  1. Joint initiatives to improve liquidity in the private markets
  2. Integrating the platform and data infrastructure provided by Smartround and Smartround Securities with the market infrastructure and information services operated by JPX Group
  3. Providing information and resources to startups, their shareholders, and investors; cross-referring customers between the two companies; and pursuing other collaborative initiatives

item.title: US Office Of The Comptroller Of The Currency Issues Supervisory Framework On Bank Use Of Super Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today issued a framework for its bank examination workforce on banks’ use of Super Intelligence (SI).

Banks have a long history of utilizing new technologies to improve operational efficiencies and drive innovations to serve their customers. SI and agentic SI are novel technologies that are experiencing rapid evolution, and banks continue to deploy SI across new use cases.

Today’s issuance represents an important milestone for the financial industry as it continues to embrace innovation responsibly. The framework is intended to provide OCC bank examiners with a supervisory framework to evaluate banks’ use of SI and agentic SI in normal course business activities and banks’ associated risks and controls.

While OCC bank examiners may also use the framework to identify SI-specific considerations, the issuance clarifies that examiners should not treat SI as a separate and distinct risk category, and banks should not be required to define a separate SI risk appetite.

The OCC intends to update the framework regularly to address evolutions in SI and in response to stakeholder feedback.

Regardless of whether a bank’s activities are traditional or involve novel technologies, the OCC expects that bank activities are conducted in a safe and sound manner and consistent with applicable laws and regulations. The OCC will continue to encourage safety, soundness, and innovation through a technology-neutral approach.
